fig-p597111-acid-dimer.svg: Two side-by-side comparisons of hydrogen bonding. Left: two acetic acid molecules, CH3COOH, face each other head to head. The O-H hydrogen of each acid is joined by a dotted hydrogen bond to the C=O oxygen of the other acid, closing a ring, so the pair is held by two hydrogen bonds. Right: two ethanol molecules, CH3CH2OH; the O-H hydrogen of one is joined by a single dotted hydrogen bond to the oxygen of the other, so the pair is held by one hydrogen bond. Lone pairs are not shown.
fig-p597148-rbc-tonicity.svg: Three red blood cells, each in a different salt solution. Left, hypotonic, 0.45 percent NaCl: blue arrows point from the solution into the cell; water moves in, and the cell is drawn swollen and round because it swells and may burst. Middle, isotonic, 0.9 percent NaCl (normal saline): pairs of arrows point both in and out, showing no net movement of water; the cell is a normal biconcave disc with a pale center. Right, hypertonic, 3 percent NaCl: arrows point out of the cell; water moves out, and the cell is drawn small with a spiky, crenated edge because it shrinks.
fig-p597140-polysaccharides.svg: Schematic comparison of three glucose polymers, each glucose unit drawn as a circle. Left, starch amylose: an unbranched chain of glucose joined by alpha 1,4 links that coils into a helix, about six glucose units per turn; digested by amylase. Middle, glycogen: a highly branched tree; straight runs are alpha 1,4 chains and each branch starts at an alpha 1,6 link, one branch point circled, with a branch about every 8 to 12 units; the many chain ends are shaded green because glucose is added or removed there. Right, cellulose: three straight, parallel chains of glucose joined by beta 1,4 links, with each unit flipped relative to its neighbor, and rows of dotted blue hydrogen bonds holding neighboring chains together in a sheet; humans cannot digest it.
fig-p597196-glycogen-branches.svg: Sketch of one glycogen molecule. A small protein, glycogenin, sits at the core on the left. A main chain of glucose units, drawn as circles, runs to the right from it; the first glucose, the reducing end, is tied to glycogenin. Straight runs are joined by alpha 1,4 links, and side chains branch off above and below the main chain, with smaller branches growing off the side chains. One branch point, where a new chain starts with an alpha 1,6 link, is circled. Every chain ends in a green non-reducing end with a free carbon 4 OH; there are many of them. A key explains that glycogen synthase adds glucose at the non-reducing ends and glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose there, so a highly branched molecule with many ends stores and releases glucose quickly.
fig-p597209-acyl-coa-numbering.svg: Two skeletal structures of a fatty acyl CoA chain, drawn as zigzag lines running left from the thioester end, which is at the right. Top, fatty acyl CoA: carbon 1 is the thioester carbon, C double-bonded to O and single-bonded to S of coenzyme A, written C(=O)-S-CoA. The carbons are numbered 1, 2, 3 and onward from that carbon. Carbon 2 is labeled alpha and carbon 3 is labeled beta; carbon 3 is highlighted as the CH2 that is oxidized to C=O in beta-oxidation. Bottom, the 3-ketoacyl CoA formed after reactions 1 to 3: the same chain with a C=O on carbon 3, the beta carbon, so 3-ketoacyl CoA and beta-ketoacyl CoA are the same compound. A dashed line between carbons 2 and 3 marks where thiolase cuts, between the alpha and beta carbons.
fig-p597144-linoleic-omega.svg: Linoleic acid, an 18-carbon fatty acid with two cis double bonds, drawn twice as the same zigzag chain with the COOH group at the left and the CH3 end at the right. Each cis double bond bends the chain. Top drawing, chemist numbering: carbons are numbered 1 to 18 starting from the COOH carbon; the double bonds are between C9 and C10 and between C12 and C13, and C12, where the last double bond starts, is highlighted. Bottom drawing, omega numbering: the same carbons are numbered omega 1 to omega 18 starting from the CH3 carbon, so C18 is omega 1 and C13 is omega 6. Omega 6 is highlighted as the first double-bonded carbon reached from the CH3 end. A note reads 18 minus 12 equals 6: omega-6.
fig-p597056-lewis-errors.svg: Four Lewis structures that students drew, each in its own box. (a) Methanol, CH3OH, as drawn: carbon bonded to three H and to O, and the O bonded to one H with three lone pairs. Corrected: the O has two lone pairs. Error: too many electrons; the drawing uses 16 electrons but methanol has 14. (b) Formaldehyde, H2C=O: carbon bonded to two H and double-bonded to O, which has two lone pairs. This one is correct: 12 electrons, carbon has four bonds, oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs. (c) Ethanethiol, CH3CH2SH, as drawn: the sulfur has two bonds and only one lone pair. Corrected: the sulfur has two lone pairs. Error: octet not satisfied; S has only 6 electrons. (d) Methylamine, as drawn: the nitrogen is bonded to the carbon and to three H, with no lone pair. Corrected: CH3NH2, nitrogen bonded to carbon and two H with one lone pair. Error: four bonds and no lone pair is the pattern of a positive nitrogen, as in CH3NH3+.
fig-p597123-lidocaine-neutral.svg: Qualitative horizontal bar chart of how much of the lidocaine is in the neutral, uncharged amine form, R3N, the only form that crosses the nerve membrane, in three places. No numbers are given. In the cartridge, which is acidic at about pH 3.5 to 6.5, the bar is very short: almost all the drug is the charged, dissolved salt R3NH+ Cl-. In healthy tissue, buffered to pH 7.4, the bar is much longer: more of the drug is neutral R3N, which crosses the nerve membrane. In an abscess or inflamed tissue, where the pH is lower than 7.4, the bar is short again: more drug stays as R3NH+, so anesthesia is slower and weaker.
